papers.title: Surveillance-Band Artificial Potential Field Guidance for USV Standoff Surveillance Under Loss of External Supervisory Communication
papers.abstract: Maritime surveillance by unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) can be degraded by external supervisory communication loss. This study formulated communication-denied maritime surveillance using a USV as a surveillance-band regulation problem, assuming that onboard navigation and relative target-position estimation remain available, and developed a surveillance-band artificial potential field (SB-APF) guidance scheme. The proposed scheme combines band-boundary restoration, desired-distance alignment, danger-zone escape, tangential surveillance, navigational-hazard avoidance, and safe-reference bias within a mode-switching structure for reacquisition (recovery into the surveillance band), maintenance, and escape-and-return. The SB-APF was evaluated against six baseline policies under 18 conditions using Monte Carlo replications with matched seeds; pairwise differences were examined using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction, effect sizes, and confidence intervals. Compared with Fast Lyapunov vector-field guidance (Fast-LVFG) with nf=60, SB-APF maintained comparable surveillance maintenance and similar first-escape timing and reduced the mean reacquisition time by approximately 39 s, whereas Fast-LVFG provided more precise desired-distance regulation. Switching stabilization and a localized hazard-normal correction reduced hazard-region entry from 7.74% to 0.56% of the hazard-present runs relative to the configuration with neither mechanism, although residual entries and mission-level costs remained. These findings suggest that surveillance-band regulation provides a viable mission-oriented guidance structure within the tested guidance-level simulation conditions.

papers.title: Experimental and Numerical Investigation of Visible-Light Characteristics of a Submerged Sphere Wake Under Wind-Wave Conditions
papers.abstract: Surface wakes generated by submerged bodies are weak in visible-light images and obscured by wind waves. Towing experiments with a submerged sphere in a large basin investigated the effects of towing speed, submergence depth, wind speed, and camera viewing angle. A linear free surface potential flow model was coupled with a directional wind-wave spectrum and an empirical relationship between surface slope and grey level. Experimental and simulated images were compared using the relative amplitude ratio R95, the texture energy fraction at intermediate scales ηM, and the spatial separability metric ΔA3. Increasing towing speed strengthened the wake and promoted a continuous wave system with a V shape; at H/D = 1.5 and a wind setting of 1 m/s, experimental ΔA3 increased from 0.107 to 22.538 percentage points over towing speeds of 0.4 to 1.0 m/s. Greater submergence generally reduced texture energy and spatial separability. Stronger wind waves masked the wake: at H/D = 1.5 and a towing speed of 1 m/s, increasing the wind setting from 0 to 4 m/s reduced experimental R95 from 3.084 to 0.979. Viewing angle altered projected wake geometry and brightness symmetry. Simulations reproduced the principal trends, although discrepancies remained in local amplitude and high-response area.

papers.title: Unmanned Underwater Vehicle Path Following Based on Improved Soft ActorCritic with Action Smoothing
papers.abstract: The deep reinforcement learning (DRL) method shows great potential in unmanned underwater vehicle (UUV) motion control. Traditional control methods rely on an accurate UUV model. However, due to the nonlinearity of the UUV model and the complex underwater environment, it is difficult to obtain an accurate model in practice. Therefore, we propose a DRL-based path-following control method for UUV. Specifically, this method integrates the Soft Actor–Critic (SAC), prioritized experience replay (PER), and policy smoothing methods to improve the generalization, tracking accuracy, and smoothness of the controller. PER assigns greater sampling weights to samples with high learning efficiency. Another major challenge in the UUV control problem arises from the action oscillations induced by the DRL policy. This problem leads to excessive wear of the actuator system and difficulty in practical applications. To address this, an improved policy regularization method is designed to promote action smoothness. In addition, a dynamic reward function that integrates tracking error, motion state, and control signals is designed to improve training efficiency. The simulation results show that improved SAC has a smooth control signal and good tracking accuracy in different waypoint configurations and uncertain disturbances.

papers.title: RGB-Derived Multi-Representation Texture Enhancement for Underwater Object Detection
papers.abstract: Underwater object detection is hindered by haze, color distortion, and weak object boundaries. This study develops MTUDNet, a YOLOv8n-based framework that combines a dehazed appearance, RGB-derived pseudo-depth, and depth-guided texture cues with frequency-spatial-channel attention and a boundary-adaptive box loss. The contribution lies in their task-oriented integration and in the boundary-discrepancy regression design; the dehazing and monocular depth estimators are adopted from prior work. Relative to YOLOv8n, MTUDNet increases mAP@0.5:0.95 by 6.6, 5.8, and 11.7 percentage points on DUO, UODD, and RUOD, respectively. It obtains 53.4% mAP@0.5:0.95 on UODD with 4.3 million detector parameters. Comparisons with U-DECN and GCC-Net show that this compact detector does not lead every accuracy metric. The 4.3 million parameters characterize the detector only; full-pipeline latency is not reported. Future work will measure complete inference time and assess pseudo-depth reliability under changing underwater conditions.

papers.title: Maritime Security and Risk Assessments—2nd Edition: From Risk Identification to Decision Support and System Resilience
papers.abstract: Maritime safety and security are increasingly shaped by dense traffic, digitised navigation, automation, cyber-physical dependencies, decarbonisation and geopolitical conflict. Deliberate attacks on civilian shipping compound the difficulty of protecting crews and assisting disabled vessels carrying hazardous cargoes in contested waters. Building on the first edition’s focus on AIS-enabled surveillance, anomaly detection, collision-risk assessment and maritime domain awareness, this second edition examines the progression from risk identification to risk-informed decision-making, validation, and system resilience. Its twelve contributions represent three research streams: (i) regional collision-risk sensing, route planning, COLREG-compliant decision-making and autonomous-system validation; (ii) human–technology interaction and data-driven accident causation; and (iii) ship safety, port resilience and maritime spatial planning. The studies convert traffic data, simulations, accident reports, and expert knowledge into evidence to support operational decisions, while revealing common limitations: limited external and prospective validation, incomplete causal identification, sparse or imbalanced data, simplified simulation assumptions, and weak integration across ship, traffic area, port and network scales. Credible implementation of these results will require trustworthy data, explicit treatment of uncertainty, human-centred assurance, interoperable validation environments, and pre-planned response and recovery arrangements for cyber-physical failures, armed attacks, and casualties caused by alternative fuels.
